Lessons.Title: Evidence, Angles, and Proof
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: State a defensible conjecture from a labelled diagram and write a complete narrative proof that vertical angles are congruent.

Verbal diagram: two distinct straight lines intersect at O. Their four rays in cyclic order are OA, OB, OC, OD, with OA opposite OC and OB opposite OD. Vertical pairs are ∠AOB and ∠COD, and ∠BOC and ∠DOA.

Proof model: ∠AOB and ∠BOC form a straight angle, so their measures sum to 180 degrees. ∠BOC and ∠COD also form a straight angle. Subtract the common m∠BOC from both equations to obtain m∠AOB=m∠COD. This is a logical deduction, not a measurement from a drawing.

Student task: supply a narrative proof in words and annotate angle pairs with reason-based equality symbols; identify a nonexample formed by adjacent rather than vertical angles. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicitly named opposite rays; true linear-pair equations; valid subtraction inference; clear conclusion/diagram labels.

Independently authored Edulytiks explanations and tasks; source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. No publisher drawings or restricted assessment answers are reproduced.

Source 19.1 Math Talk Supplementary Angles: intersect two lines at O with adjacent measures 70° and 110°, and require a discussion of all four angles and the 180° linear-pair fact. Original first-party verbal diagram replaces the unverified publisher figures; pupils justify rather than measure a picture.

Source 19.2 That Can't Be Right, Can It?: line l with ray r creates adjacent supplementary angles α and β. Students FIRST label the rays and their interior bisectors and restate the ambiguous conjecture precisely, THEN prove the angle between the two bisectors is (α+β)/2=90°. The proof applies to all nondegenerate α,β>0 with α+β=180°, not only a numerical example.

Source 19.3 Convince Me: label two intersecting lines and independently write a connected NARRATIVE proof that vertical angles agree. One proof uses a 180° rotation about their intersection, carrying both boundary rays to opposite rays; another uses α+β=180° and β+γ=180° to conclude α=γ. Explain why adjacent supplementary angles are not automatically congruent. A two-column outline or mere measured 70° is not a complete narrative proof.

Optional source conjecture counterexample: the first values of maximum regions formed by joining n points on a circle can appear to double, but at n=6 the maximal region count is 31 rather than 32 for chords in general position. Discuss why examples do not prove a universal theorem; optional only, not scored as mandatory proof.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertical angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: The opposite angle pair formed by intersecting lines, sharing a vertex but no side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Show equality using linear pairs or a valid rigid transformation.
KeyConcepts.Example: If one angle is 47 degrees, its vertical angle is 47 degrees.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear pair
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two adjacent angles whose nonshared sides are opposite rays and therefore sum to 180 degrees.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify the opposite rays before asserting supplementary measures.

KeyConcepts.Title: Narrative proof
KeyConcepts.Definition: A connected argument deriving a claim from definitions or known results with a reason at every step.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish observed pattern, conjecture and justified theorem.
KeyConcepts.Example: Subtracting equal expressions for a straight angle proves the vertical-angle equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove vertical angles
WorkedExamples.Question: Two lines AC and BD intersect at O. Prove ∠AOB≅∠COD.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use two linear-pair equations that share the angle BOC.
Steps: Since OA and OC are opposite rays, m∠AOB+m∠BOC=180°.
Since OB and OD are opposite rays, m∠BOC+m∠COD=180°.
Both sums equal 180°, so m∠AOB+m∠BOC=m∠BOC+m∠COD.
Subtract m∠BOC to conclude m∠AOB=m∠COD.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The vertical angles ∠AOB and ∠COD are congruent.
WorkedExamples.Check: No parallel-line assumption or protractor measurement is needed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find angles and justify
WorkedExamples.Question: At intersecting lines, an angle is 62°. Find its adjacent and vertical angles.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use supplementary linear pairs and vertical-angle equality.
Steps: The vertical angle is congruent, hence 62°.
Each adjacent angle forms a linear pair with the 62° angle.
Each adjacent measure is 180°−62°=118°.
Opposite adjacent angles are both 118°, consistent with vertical-angle equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a false angle proof
WorkedExamples.Question: A student says ∠AOB=∠BOC because they share a vertex. Is this justified?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check whether shared-vertex property implies equality.
Steps: Sharing O is common to all four angles at intersecting lines.
Adjacent angles can measure 62° and 118° while sharing O.
Only an actual vertical pair is guaranteed congruent here.
A shared vertex alone is insufficient.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; sharing a vertex does not imply congruent angles.
WorkedExamples.Check: Provide a valid diagram with unequal adjacent angles to disprove the claim.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Presenting matching-looking angles as the proof.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Angle appearance and image proportions are not precise mathematical evidence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write the linear-pair equations and deduct the shared term.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing adjacent angles with vertical angles.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Adjacent angles generally sum to 180°, rather than necessarily being equal.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Locate opposite rays and confirm the pair shares no ray.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: State a defensible conjecture from a labelled diagram and write a complete narrative proof that vertical angles are congruent.
Every proof needs explicit hypotheses, logical reasons and a conclusion; attractive diagrams are not proof.
The authentic proof, construction or open explanation is teacher-scored; there is no numeric proxy auto-grade.

Lessons.Title: Transformations, Transversals, and Proof
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove that a transversal cutting two distinct parallel lines creates congruent corresponding angles and congruent alternate interior angles, using rigid transformations and their geometric invariants.

Verbal diagram: horizontal parallels ℓ:y=0 and m:y=3 are crossed by the same transversal t. Label each intersection and specify which ray directions form corresponding or alternate interior angles. A mere equal-looking figure without a verified parallel assumption does not justify the theorem.

Transformational reasoning: translating by the directed segment along transversal t between intersections maps ℓ to m because lines parallel to ℓ through the target intersection are unique. It also maps t to itself as an infinite line, so corresponding angle ray pairs align. A 180-degree rotation about the midpoint between the intersections exchanges the two intersections, maps each parallel line to the other, and maps rays on t into opposite rays, explaining alternate-interior correspondence.

Student task: present both narrative proof mechanisms, then construct a counterexample when lines are not parallel. Teacher rubric (0–4): verified parallel hypotheses; valid translation/half-turn correspondence; unambiguous angle labels; logical conclusion/counterexample. Source-style written proofs cannot be replaced by automatically graded angle guesses.

Independently authored Edulytiks explanations and tasks; source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. No publisher drawings or restricted assessment answers are reproduced.

20.1 Source Math Talk: parallel lines l:y=0 and m:y=3 cut by transversal t:y=x at B(0,0) and C(3,3). Label ray-oriented corresponding and alternate interior angle pairs, explain their measures before relying on theorems.

20.2 Source Make a Mark? Give a Reason: translate l and transversal by directed segment BC=(3,3), mapping l onto m and t onto itself; corresponding angles and ray directions are preserved. Partners exchange and critique complete narrative explanations.

20.3 Source An Alternate Explanation: rotate 180° about M=(1.5,1.5), midpoint of BC, exchanging B/C and two parallel lines and reversing transversal rays, hence alternate interior angles are congruent. A centre on a line maps it to itself; a centre off maps it to a distinct parallel line.
Source practice converse: equal alternate interior angles imply coplanar lines parallel. The argument does not depend on a particular sample angle such as 40 degrees.

KeyConcepts.Title: Corresponding angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Angles in the same relative position where a transversal meets two lines.
KeyConcepts.Rule: They are congruent when the lines are parallel, via translation aligning intersections.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 40° corresponding angle across a parallel pair is also 40°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Alternate interior angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Interior angles on opposite sides of a transversal at two intersections.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For parallel lines these are congruent; a half-turn between intersections supplies a rigid-motion justification.
KeyConcepts.Example: An interior angle of 61° has corresponding alternate-interior angle 61°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel hypothesis
KeyConcepts.Definition: A geometric condition requiring two coplanar straight lines not to intersect.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The corresponding/alternate interior congruence implication needs the parallel condition.
KeyConcepts.Example: If two nonparallel lines cross one transversal, their same-position angles need not agree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove corresponding-angle equality
WorkedExamples.Question: Lines ℓ and m are parallel and t meets them at X and Y. Why are corresponding angles congruent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Translate by the directed segment XY along the transversal.
Steps: Translation T taking X to Y maps line t onto itself.
T maps ℓ to a parallel line through Y.
Because m is the unique line parallel to ℓ through Y, T(ℓ)=m.
The image of each angle ray at X lies along its corresponding ray at Y.
Translation preserves angle measure, so the corresponding angles are congruent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Corresponding angles are equal when ℓ∥m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Explicitly uses uniqueness of a parallel through Y and the directed translation along t.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove alternate-interior equality
WorkedExamples.Question: Why are alternate interior angles equal when t crosses parallels at X and Y?
WorkedExamples.Method: Rotate the plane 180° about midpoint M of XY.
Steps: A half-turn about M sends X to Y and sends line t to itself.
A half-turn sends ℓ to a parallel line through Y, hence to m.
Interior rays at X map to opposite-side interior rays at Y.
Rigid rotation preserves angle measures, so the alternate-interior angle pair is congruent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Alternate interior angles are congruent under parallel-line hypotheses.
WorkedExamples.Check: A 180° half-turn is an isometry with a fixed centre M.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check the role of parallel lines
WorkedExamples.Question: Two different lines cross a transversal, creating angles 45° and 60° in corresponding positions. Can the lines be parallel?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the contrapositive of the corresponding-angle theorem.
Steps: Parallel lines would force their corresponding angles to be congruent.
The given angles 45° and 60° are unequal.
Therefore the two lines cannot be parallel.
No angle measure is inferred from a picture; only the stated measures are used.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, the lines are not parallel.
WorkedExamples.Check: The rule requires matching corresponding positions and actual measured values.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using corresponding-angle equality without stating the lines are parallel.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: With nonparallel lines, corresponding angles are not necessarily congruent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State and verify ℓ∥m before the transformation proof.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming that any translation maps one line to any other line through Y.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Translations preserve direction; only the parallel through Y is obtained.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the uniqueness of the parallel through Y to identify the image line.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Prove that a transversal cutting two distinct parallel lines creates congruent corresponding angles and congruent alternate interior angles, using rigid transformations and their geometric invariants.
Every proof needs explicit hypotheses, logical reasons and a conclusion; attractive diagrams are not proof.
The authentic proof, construction or open explanation is teacher-scored; there is no numeric proxy auto-grade.

Lessons.Title: One Hundred and Eighty
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove that the interior angles of every nondegenerate Euclidean triangle sum to 180 degrees, using a parallel construction and the established alternate-interior-angle theorem.

Verbal diagram: triangle ABC has three noncollinear vertices. Through A draw a line ℓ parallel to BC; the rays AB and AC divide the straight angle at A into three adjacent angles, with two outer angles congruent to interior angles at B and C by the parallel-transversal theorem.

The theorem depends on Euclidean geometry and a genuine triangle: collinear 'vertices' form a degenerate segment, not a nondegenerate triangle. The familiar 180° is not a universal theorem on curved surfaces.

Student task: write a narrative proof for an acute, obtuse or right triangle and separately critique an argument that incorrectly assumes two lines parallel. Teacher rubric (0–4): valid parallel construction; correct corresponding/alternate-angle matches; precise straight-angle sum; a general statement independent of measured examples. The full proof is human reviewed.

Independently authored Edulytiks explanations and tasks; source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. No publisher drawings or restricted assessment answers are reproduced.

21.1 What Went Wrong?: lines l and m are NOT parallel and are crossed by a transversal. Tyler assumes corresponding angles must agree after translating one vertex onto another. Partners inspect each of the four stated justifications; the crucial false step is claiming the image of line l (parallel to l) lies on the distinct nonparallel line m. No corresponding-angle equality follows without parallel lines.

21.2 Triangle Angle Sum One Way: for any nondegenerate triangle ABC mark midpoints of AB and AC. A 180-degree turn of the triangle about each of those midpoints sends line BC to a line through A parallel to BC. The two images coincide by uniqueness of the parallel through A. The corresponding alternate-interior angles at A give measures b and c beside original angle a; these form a straight angle a+b+c=180°. This is a full narrative proof, not a diagram measurement.

21.3 Triangle Angle Sum Another Way: translate ABC by directed segment B→C, label all image vertices; then translate the image so A' maps to C, labelling second-stage vertices. Track transformed rays and use rigidity to place the three original angle measures consecutively around a straight line at C. Because the translated corresponding side lines are parallel, a+b+c=180° for every noncollinear Euclidean triangle. Students give a second independent narrative proof.

Optional extension: the 180-degree sum is Euclidean; a spherical triangle using the North Pole and two equatorial points separated by 90° has three right angles, summing 270°. This does not invalidate the Euclidean proof and is not part of required scoring.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle angle sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: In a nondegenerate triangle in the Euclidean plane, its three interior angles total 180 degrees.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Through a vertex construct a parallel to the opposite side and use alternate-interior-angle equality.
KeyConcepts.Example: If angles A and B are 50° and 60°, angle C is 70°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel through a vertex
KeyConcepts.Definition: There exists exactly one line through A parallel to BC in Euclidean geometry.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify the two transversal intersections and correct paired angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: AB and AC act as two transversals of ℓ∥BC.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exterior angle
KeyConcepts.Definition: An angle adjacent to one triangle interior angle along an extended side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Its measure equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, following the 180° theorem.
KeyConcepts.Example: If remote interior angles are 35° and 65°, the exterior angle is 100°.

WorkedExamples.Title: General angle-sum proof
WorkedExamples.Question: Prove ∠A+∠B+∠C=180° for any triangle ABC.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw a parallel to BC through A and use transversal angles.
Steps: Because A,B,C are noncollinear, triangle ABC is well defined.
Draw line ℓ through A parallel to BC.
By alternate-interior angles with transversal AB, one outer angle at A equals ∠B.
By alternate-interior angles with transversal AC, the other outer angle at A equals ∠C.
These two outer angles and interior ∠A form a straight angle, summing to 180°.
WorkedExamples.Check: The proof makes no assumptions about acute, right or obtuse angle types.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute third angle with proof
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle has two angles 37° and 83°. Find the third.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the proven triangle angle-sum theorem.
Steps: The three interior angles sum to 180°.
Known angles total 37°+83°=120°.
Unknown measure is 180°−120°=60°.
All three are strictly between 0° and 180°, so the data are consistent with a nondegenerate triangle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exterior angle theorem
WorkedExamples.Question: Remote interior angles are 35° and 65°. Find the exterior angle at the third vertex.
Steps: The third interior angle is 180°−(35°+65°)=80°.
The exterior angle adjacent to it forms a straight angle.
Exterior angle is 180°−80°=100°.
Therefore it equals 35°+65°, the two remote interior angles.
WorkedExamples.Check: The third interior angle and adjacent exterior total 180°.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming the triangle sum from measuring one sketch.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Measurements are approximate and one example cannot prove a universal theorem.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a valid Euclidean parallel construction and exact angle equalities.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the parallel-transversal theorem on lines not known parallel.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Corresponding or alternate interior angles may not be congruent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Construct ℓ∥BC explicitly before identifying equal angles.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Prove that the interior angles of every nondegenerate Euclidean triangle sum to 180 degrees, using a parallel construction and the established alternate-interior-angle theorem.
Every proof needs explicit hypotheses, logical reasons and a conclusion; attractive diagrams are not proof.
The authentic proof, construction or open explanation is teacher-scored; there is no numeric proxy auto-grade.

Lessons.Title: Now What Can You Build?
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Design a novel reproducible geometric pattern using straightedge-and-compass techniques and communicate enough precise instructions for another student to reconstruct it.

This is explicitly optional source enrichment: it extends earlier construction tasks and requires original pattern creation. The original source includes designs used with third-party permission; Edulytiks does not copy those drawings. An original written construction and peer-produced replica are the authentic assessment evidence.

First-party visual concept (verbal diagram): begin with segment AB of positive length; construct equilateral triangle ABC; from its three vertices draw circles of the same radius AB/3 if marked by an independently constructed trisection or choose radius AB/2 via its midpoint construction. Connect circle intersection marks only when they exist and label every step.

Student task: invent a two- or three-stage compound pattern incorporating at least one exact perpendicular bisector, one pair of congruent circles and one nontrivial line or rotational symmetry. Write the steps without relying on a picture and exchange with a peer who attempts the construction. Teacher rubric (0–4): legal precise operations, reproducibility and labelled dependencies, mathematical justification, and peer-feedback revision. This is NOT a machine-gradable numeric question.

Independently authored Edulytiks explanations and tasks; source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), CC BY 4.0. No publisher drawings or restricted assessment answers are reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constructible pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pattern whose objects can be obtained from the stated inputs by permitted compass/straightedge operations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify each centre, copied length, intersection and subsequent connection.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two equal-radius circles centred at distinct A and B produce two intersection points if their radii are greater than AB/2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Precision and source independence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Reproducible procedures must specify invariant geometry without copying protected decorative artwork.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use independently authored labelled objects and explain the underlying relationships.
KeyConcepts.Example: A repeated triangle pattern can be described by equal-radius intersections rather than a publisher screenshot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Authentic assessment
KeyConcepts.Definition: Evidence includes original construction, written procedure, peer replication and correction of an ambiguity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A teacher must review the actual figures and procedural reasoning.
KeyConcepts.Example: ‘Draw a circle’ is insufficient until centre and radius are specified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original two-circle flower seed
WorkedExamples.Question: Create a symmetric six-vertex starting pattern from centre O and point A, OA>0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the compass opening OA around one fixed circle.
Steps: Draw circle k centred at O through A.
Keep compass opening OA and use A as centre to mark the next intersection B on k.
Move the compass centre to B to mark C, choosing the next counterclockwise intersection.
Repeat until A,B,C,D,E,F are six successive vertices.
Join consecutive vertices: six central angles of 60° complete one full revolution.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A regular hexagon ABCDEF inscribed in k provides a symmetric skeleton for a new design.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks exact stepping and the direction of selected intersections, not appearance alone.

WorkedExamples.Title: Decorate while preserving a mirror
WorkedExamples.Question: Given an equilateral triangle ABC, how can you make a symmetric original pattern with equal circles at the vertices?
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose a common radius and use circles centred at each vertex.
Steps: Construct a nondegenerate equilateral triangle ABC.
Construct the midpoint M of AB with its perpendicular bisector, setting radius r=AM=AB/2.
Without changing compass opening r, draw circles centred A,B,C.
Every reflection axis of the equilateral triangle permutes the three equal circles, so the combined design remains reflection-symmetric.
WorkedExamples.Answer: An equilateral triangle with three equal-radius vertex-centred circles has three reflection axes.
WorkedExamples.Check: No image is needed to justify invariance: each symmetry permutes the three centres and preserves their radii.

WorkedExamples.Title: Repair an unreproducible instruction
WorkedExamples.Question: A peer says ‘draw circles at the corners and join the nice intersections’. Why does this fail?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify unspecified data and rewrite as exact tool directions.
Steps: ‘Corners’ needs a named initial polygon and ordered vertex labels.
Circles need named centres and a single defined radius or individually defined radii.
An intersection needs a unique label and specification of which of two possible crossings to select.
Rewrite using the equilateral triangle ABC, circle centres A,B,C, radius AB/2 and explicit intersection naming or a permissible choice.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The revised procedure provides constructible inputs and unambiguous dependencies.
WorkedExamples.Check: Have another student reconstruct it from words alone, noting any remaining choice that changes the figure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Leaving centre, radius or intersection choice implicit.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The reader cannot determine a unique reproducible configuration.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label each given object and write exact consecutive compass/straightedge steps.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Scoring a creative drawing only with a numeric answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It does not measure authorship, construction legality, precision, reflection symmetry or peer reproduction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use submitted construction plus written instructions and teacher-reviewed rubric.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: Design a novel reproducible geometric pattern using straightedge-and-compass techniques and communicate enough precise instructions for another student to reconstruct it.
Every proof needs explicit hypotheses, logical reasons and a conclusion; attractive diagrams are not proof.
The authentic proof, construction or open explanation is teacher-scored; there is no numeric proxy auto-grade.
